guidance: CIDR aggregation only: it turns a list of IPv4 prefixes into the minimal set of routes covering the same addresses. It is not a subnet calculator, an address-planning tool, a VLSM allocation planner or a routing policy simulator.
method: Every IPv4 prefix is held as an inclusive integer range: its first address is its value rounded down to a multiple of its block size 2^(32-length), and its last is that plus the size minus one, so a prefix with host bits set is refused instead of being guessed at. Duplicates are dropped, then any prefix already inside a broader one, and the survivors are merged by repeatedly folding two prefixes of the same length that are aligned siblings into their parent, until no pair can merge. The result is the minimal set of CIDR blocks covering exactly the input addresses, so nothing extra is announced. Addresses covered is the sum of the aggregate block sizes; the smallest covering supernet is the longest common prefix of the lowest and highest address, its size is 2^(32-length) and the addresses it adds are its size minus the covered count. Contiguity is tested by merging the aggregate blocks into runs: one run means the set is a single contiguous range, and otherwise the run boundaries give the number of gaps and the first gap. Input is up to 64 prefixes as CIDR text, separated by newlines, spaces, commas or semicolons; prefix lengths run from 0 to 32, octets must be decimal 0 to 255 without leading zeros, IPv6 is refused, and every error names the line and the prefix. The model covers IPv4 only and takes no view of routing policy: it counts no AS paths, metrics, longest-prefix behaviour or prefix origin, and announcing the covering supernet would also announce the gaps between the blocks. It reads no routing table, keeps no record, and runs entirely in the browser with no uploads, accounts or network access.
